cues.text: Put Nell exactly on Marshall's line. Exactly on it. The money coming in is precisely enough to cover everything, including the cost of her money.
Marshall says she should be indifferent. Build, or do not build. It makes no difference either way.
Hang on. There is a third thing she could do, and neither of those is it.
Give her one very simple plan. Wait a fixed stretch of time.
Then look at the money coming in.
If it is above the line, build. If it is not, never build. It is not even the best plan — it is just a plan, and it is enough to make the point.
Now watch what the future might do, starting from that point. Here are five futures. Nobody knows which one happens. Some end high. Some end low.
In the two futures that end high, she looks, she sees the money is well above the line, and she builds. She gains.
In the two that end low, she looks, and she does not build. She gains nothing.
But look at that again, because everything turns on it. She gains nothing — and she loses nothing.
Two outcomes that pay something. Three that pay nothing at all — but cost nothing either.
Weigh each by how likely it is, and add them up. The answer is bigger than nothing. It cannot be anything else.
Here is the sentence this chapter exists for. Waiting cuts off the bad half, and keeps the good half.
That selective removal of risk is what waiting is worth.
This is the most counter-intuitive part of the chapter, so I am going to say it twice. It has nothing whatsoever to do with disliking risk.
Nell is assumed not to mind risk at all. She would take a fair gamble without blinking. And she still waits.
The trade she is making is between risk now and risk later. It is about timing, not nerves.

gains + zeros > nothing, so waiting wins
